Habitation
hab-i-tā'shun
n. (a dwelling place; rendering Hebrew maon, Greek katoiketerion)
From the Latin habitatio, from habito, to dwell, a frequentative of habeo, to have — to dwell is to keep on having a place. Hebrew maon is a lair or dwelling, and zebul a lofty residence, the word Solomon used of the temple he had built.

Biblical Definition

Habitation is the settled dwelling place of a person, and Scripture uses it with striking symmetry: God has one, angels had one, and the church becomes one. Of God the word is used of heaven, from which he governs: “From the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth” (Psalm 33:14), and Israel prays “Look down from thy holy habitation, from heaven, and bless thy people Israel” (Deuteronomy 26:15). Of the fallen angels it marks the enormity of their apostasy: they “kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation” (Jude 1:6) — creatures abandoning the station God assigned them, which is the essence of that sin and of every sin patterned after it. Then the astonishing turn: what God has in heaven he takes up among men, and not in a building. Paul tells the Ephesians that they are “builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22). The tabernacle in the wilderness and the temple on Zion were shadows of this; the substance is a people. The line runs from Eden through the wilderness tent and the stone temple to the incarnate Word who tabernacled among us, to the indwelt church, and ends in the city where God shall dwell with men and be their God.

Webster 1828 Definition

A settled dwelling place. Scripture gives one to God in heaven, records that the fallen angels abandoned theirs, and then makes the church itself an habitation of God through the Spirit.

expand to see more

HABITATION, n. [L. habitatio, from habito, to dwell.] Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling.

2. Place of abode; a settled dwelling; a mansion; a residence.

3. The abode of God; as, thy holy habitation, Deut. 26.

4. The station or estate assigned to a creature; as, the angels left their own habitation, Jude 6.

5. In Scripture, of the church, builded together for an habitation of God, Eph. 2.

Key Scripture

Psalm 33:14 — "From the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth."

Deuteronomy 26:15 — "Look down from thy holy habitation, from heaven, and bless thy people Israel, and the land which thou hast given us, as thou swarest unto our fathers, a land that floweth with milk and honey."

Jude 1:6 — "And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day."

Ephesians 2:22 — "In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit."

Modern Corruption

Church buildings are still commonly called God's house, and the New Testament reassigns the term to the people. The building is a convenience; the habitation is the congregation.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure on this word comes from long habit inside the church rather than from outside it. When the sanctuary is spoken of as the house of God in a sense the New Testament reserves for the assembly, small distortions follow: reverence attaches to furniture, giving flows to masonry ahead of ministry, and a congregation scattered by fire or persecution feels it has lost God's dwelling when in fact the dwelling walked out of the doors.

The principle to recover is Ephesians 2:22 read alongside Jude 1:6. God's habitation is now a people built together, which raises the stakes of church membership and of division far above what most reckon; to split a congregation carelessly is to take a hammer to the place where God has chosen to live. And Jude's angels warn from the other side: a creature who leaves the station God appointed him falls, however exalted the station was. Both texts press the same point, that dwelling where God has put you is not a small part of godliness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew maon is a dwelling or lair, zebul an exalted residence, and mishkan the tabernacle, from shakan, to dwell. Greek katoiketerion is a settled habitation and skenoo is to pitch a tent, John's verb for the incarnation.

expand to see more

Hebrew maon (H4583) — habitation, dwelling, den; used of God's heavenly abode.

Hebrew zebul (H2073) — a lofty residence; Solomon's word for the house he built.

Hebrew mishkan (H4908) — tabernacle, dwelling place; from shakan, to settle down.

Greek katoiketerion (G2732) — a settled habitation; the church in Ephesians 2:22.

Greek skenoo (G4637) — to pitch a tent, to tabernacle; the Word dwelt among us.

Usage

"Of heaven as God's dwelling: from the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth (Psalm 33:14)."

"Of angels who abandoned their station: kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation (Jude 1:6)."

"Of the church as God's dwelling: builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit (Ephesians 2:22)."
